close_reason: Positive finding: sequential URL fetch in document order
description:
src/async_crl.rs:46-54, src/async_ocsp.rs:54-57: explicit comments rejecting parallel fan-out via futures::join_all. The reasoning: 'RFC 5280 §6.3.3 path-validation CRL checking is described as a per-CDP-URL sequence; mirroring that here preserves the no-CRL-fetched-after-first-success property that operators rely on for rate-limit / quota planning.'

What a future contributor will incorrectly suggest:

1. 'Fan out the URL fetches in parallel; the async runtime is the whole point of async.' — Misunderstands the contract. The first-success-wins property is consumer-observable: an operator running validations against their own internal CDP+OCSP responders relies on 'one cert generates at most one HTTP fetch per protocol' for capacity planning. Fanning out makes that observable contract 'one cert generates up to N HTTP fetches', changing the operator-observable load profile.

2. 'Race the first two URLs in parallel to reduce p99 latency.' — Hedged requests are a real optimization for some workloads. But the workload pattern here is 'fetch a CRL once, cache it, every subsequent check is cached'. The cache amortizes; hedged requests cost responder load on every cache miss. The cost ratio rarely favors hedging.

Defending this decision: the design choice is explicit, comment is in the code, the trade-off is recorded. If a consumer's specific workload wants hedging, they implement their own AsyncRevocationFetcher that does it; the wrapper above stays serial.
title: Async fetcher serializes URLs in document order (no futures::join_all fan-out)
